notes.claim: The number e is a fixed constant like π, approximately 2.71828, so it is a number to work with rather than a variable.
A logarithm answers "what power?": the base 2 logarithm of 32 is 5 because 5 is the exponent applied to 2 to get 32.
In exponential change the output is multiplied by the same factor, called the growth factor, each time the input goes up by one.
A growth factor larger than one makes the quantity grow and one less than one makes it shrink.
In exponential growth the rate of growth is proportional to the current value, so growth speeds up as the amount grows.
Dividing 72 by the growth rate in percent gives the approximate doubling time (the rule of 72), a heuristic the authors suggest educators teach.
With a 100% rate over a period, simple interest doubles the money but continually compounding interest multiplies it by e.
e is a fixed constant like π, approximately 2.71828.
In exponential growth the rate of growth is proportional to the current value.
RC is the time in which a discharging capacitor's charge drops to 1/e of its starting value, and it has dimensions of time, so it is called the time constant.
In the first time constant after the switch is closed, a discharging capacitor's voltage falls to 0.368 of its initial value.
Newton's law of cooling says an object cools or warms at a rate proportional to the gap between its temperature and the surroundings' temperature.
Newton's law of cooling holds only for very small temperature differences, so a hot part follows the capacitor-like curve only approximately.
In exponential decay the rate of change is proportional to the current value.
In insulation testing the capacitive charging current quickly falls to zero, the same shrinking charging current as a capacitor charging through a resistor (Megger, notes 7.3).
A trade tutorial (SECONDARY) treats a capacitor as fully charged after five time constants, at 99.3%: a convention, since it never reaches 100% (notes 4.4).
IEC 60831, as a trade page reports it (SECONDARY), requires power factor correction capacitors to discharge to below 75 V within 3 minutes (notes 7.2).
A logarithm gives an exponent: the base 2 logarithm of 32 is 5 because 5 is the exponent applied to 2 to get 32.
The logarithm with base e is called the natural logarithm, written ln.
The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logs of its factors.
In the log system multiplication becomes addition and division subtraction, and powers become multiplication, which is why decibel gains of stages add.
A decibel is 10 times the common logarithm of a power ratio (added for i5's decibel screens).
Engine-room sound readings are taken in decibels with A-weighting, dB(A) (added for i5's decibel screen).
When an exponential equation cannot be rewritten with a common base, it is solved by taking the logarithm of each side.
Once the exponential term is isolated, take the logarithm of both sides, then use the power rule to bring the unknown down as a factor.
For i6: dividing 72 by the growth rate in percent gives the approximate doubling time (the rule of 72), a check on the exact doubling time.
On a log-log graph the slope is the exponent n, so plotting log y against log x turns a power law into a straight line.
A-level maths expects logarithmic graphs to estimate the constants in y = ax^n and y = kb^x from data.
The case n = 1 of pV^n = constant is the isothermal expansion, where P1V1 = P2V2.
Gas kept at constant temperature has pressure and volume varying so that PV is constant, which is Boyle's Law.
The work done by n moles of ideal gas expanding reversibly and isothermally is nRT ln(V2/V1).
The special case n = 1 of pV^n = constant is the isothermal expansion, where the work integral gives a natural logarithm.

The add-one-to-the-power, divide-by-the-power rule cannot integrate certain terms, because adding one to their power gives 0 (source's equation symbols did not come through: the terms are powers of -1).
The E12 series of preferred resistor values (IEC 60063) runs 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82 ohms in each decade: twelve values per × 10. For i8's analogy.
1 bar = 0.1 MPa = 100 kPa. For i8's practice (bar times litres gives hundreds of joules).
